description:
Websites have been taken down worldwide after critical weaknesses were revealed in a programming language which powers much of the internet.  Governments and agencies are urging websites to address the problem immediately. 

The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language. The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security experts saying are were the most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered by the technology, which is reshaping the cyber security landscape.

The US National Security Agency issued a warning for organisations to take their systems offline if they are unable to immediately apply a fix, which has now been issued.   The governments of France and Finland were among those ordering shut down of some web services, along with many private organisations around the world.  Japan’s prime minister urged people to check if their publicly accessible websites ran on PHP. 
 
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and
title: Websites taken down worldwide as AI reveals critical cyber-security threat | BBC News

author: BBC News
description:
Can Ukraine still rely on America?

More than 80 years after the Yalta conference reshaped post-war Europe, some observers fear a new era of great-power diplomacy could once again shape the continent's future. Reports of a possible meeting between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have prompted questions about what role Ukraine would play in any discussion about ending the war.

The speculation comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Washington and Kyiv. From disputes over Starlink access to growing concerns about Trump's outreach to Moscow, Ukrainian officials worry they are losing influence with their most powerful ally. 

At the centre of the debate is a simple question: does Trump see Ukraine as an indispensable partner, or an obstacle to broader deals with Russia? 

The Global Story’s Tristan Redman speaks to Simon Shuster of The Atlantic about the state of the war, the future of US support and why Kyiv is increasingly worried about being left out of the r
title: Is Ukraine being shut out of its own future? | The Global Story

author: BBC News
description:
As US envoy Steve Witkoff meets Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, Ukrainians fear that President Donald Trump will side with Moscow in talks to end the war in Ukraine. Earlier, Mr Trump suggested it was up to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to end the conflict, saying he "could have made a deal two years ago". 

A US official says Mr Putin has now accepted a proposal for a technical-level trilateral meeting with Ukraine. But the Russian leader has also reportedly proposed talks with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. It is not clear whether President Zelensky would be involved in those discussions. 

Meanwhile, Russia has said it will release Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher detained by Russian forces four years ago in occupied Ukraine. Some analysts have said this decision - and Mr Putin's offer to help end the war in Iran - are attempts to curry greater favour with President Trump.

Filmmaker Jenny Krakowski set herself a challenge: make a feature-length film entirely with AI.

description:
The US midterms are usually swayed by domestic matters like economy and the cost of living. They’re often a pulse check on voter sentiment towards the incumbent party or a reflection of local political battles and regional trends. 
 
Rarely are they impassioned referendums on a specific foreign policy issue. But for some voters this year in Michigan — where Democrat hopeful Abdul El-Sayed is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers — the Senate race is shaping up to be just that. 
 
Two weeks out from the crucial polling day, The Global Story’s Asma Khalid shares her reporting from Michigan, where a debate among Democrats over the conflicts in the Middle East has become a touchstone issue, especially among the state’s large Arab American and Jewish communities.

Israel's election is taking place next Tuesday, to elect a new government, in the first election since the 7 October Hamas attacks three years ago.  
 
More than half a million first-time voters are among those due to cast their ballots.  
 
The vote is seen by many voters as an existential decision on the country’s future identity and security.
 
Surveys suggest that around three quarters of new voters see themselves as “right or centre right” – and that Israel’s far-right parties are among those benefitting. 
 
The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson has been speaking with Gen Z voters in Israel.

description:
A £3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.
 
The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.
 
At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.
 
It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the £3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

Australian MP Helen Haines has had both her legs amputated after being allegedly attacked with a car.
 
Haines received severe injuries after being struck in what police say was a targeted incident outside her electoral office in Wangaratta on Monday.
 
During a press conference, her husband, Phil, confirmed she lost both but added "she is alive and stable".
 
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
 
Police have not ruled out additional charges, including attempted murder.

author: BBC News
description:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a £45,000 illegal working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine if our undercover reporter could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone or giving false information to the Home Oﬃce.

At least £150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal working fines, according to Home Oﬃce figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way illegal working fines are issued and collected.
